1963 Chevrolet Sitting on a Trailer Beg for Restoration if You Don't Get Scared Easily
17 photos
Photo: eBay seller lamonte6447
1963 is the year, and rough is the term that describes it best. This 1963 Chevrolet Impala is here because it’s dreaming about the same thing as many other abandoned classics.
The car needs a complete restoration, but before anything else, it must convince an Internet stranger to take it home. That’s why the owner posted it on eBay, where the car should sell by this time next month.
The owner doesn’t reveal many specifics about this 1963 Chevrolet, probably hoping that the photos in the gallery tell the whole story. At some level, they do, but they also leave many questions without an answer.
Photo: eBay seller lamonte6447 1963 was such a fantastic year for Chevrolet , and the sales recorded by the company speak for themselves. The GM brand sold no more, no less than 1.57 million full-size cars, and the Impala accounted for over 50% of this number. Over 832,000 Chevrolet buyers ordered an Impala, and the best thing about this number was that the V8 engines accounted for an impressive number.
More than 735,000 Impalas left the factory with a V8 engine, and eventually, V8 power represented over 1.1 million Chevrolets sold this year.
The increased demand for V8 engines made sense, especially because the Super Sport was becoming a more popular name in the Chevrolet lineup. Only 153,000 Impalas rolled off the assembly line with the SS package.
Chevrolet continued to focus on a mix of engines that included both six-cylinder units and V8s power. The base choice was a 230ci unit with 140 horsepower, while the foray into the V8 lineup started with a 283 Turbo-Fire rated at 195 horsepower.
A 327 small-block configuration rated at 250 horsepower was a very popular choice, but customers who didn’t want to stick with this setup and wanted more power could get an upgraded version that was fitted with solid lifters and which developed 340 horsepower.
The top choice was a 409 big-block engine that produced 400 or 425 horsepower. Chevrolet also offered the Z11 drag pack package, which was rated at over 500 horsepower and carried a super-hefty price tag of $1,245. It included dual four-barrel carburetors, dual exhausts, high-lift cams, solid lifters, and an impressive 13.5:1 compression ratio.
Photo: eBay seller lamonte6447 This Impala isn’t as impressive as a Z11-powered specimen, but on the plus side, it still seems to have an engine under the hood.
This means it might still be in good mechanical shape, but considering the owner did not include any other specifics in their listing, the only option is to call them and ask all these questions. It looks to be a 327, but no other details are available, so it’s unclear if this is the original unit.
If it is, I wouldn’t expect it to be working, though a good mechanic should be able to decrypt the full story with a quick inspection.
Other than that, you don’t have to be a diehard restoration guy to figure out the rest of the details. The thick layer of dust suggests this Impala has recently been pulled from storage, while the rust and the huge floors that let clean air come through indicate that it has probably spent more than just a few years in the same place.
This could be a barn find pulled after decades, and that’s why it’s such a shame that the owner did not include additional details and maybe more detailed photos.
Photo: eBay seller lamonte6447 While some parts are obviously required, including a gas tank, the car looks fairly complete. Obviously, not everything is in condition that would allow a restoration guy to retain them after the full refresh, but on the plus side, you won’t spend countless hours online looking for parts.
It’s pretty clear that restoring this Impala won’t be easy, and I think that you need a good metal guy to fix those massive holes before anything else.
It’s time to talk money, as this is one of the most important things about a rough Chevrolet whose long-term objective is to return to the road one day.
Photo: eBay seller lamonte6447 The owner listed the car with a $6,300 price tag, but they also enabled the Make Offer option. This is typically a good sign, as it’s an indication that the owner is open to other offers, so you can use this button if you’re interested in the car but have another deal in mind.
I still recommend that potential buyers call the seller and arrange an in-person inspection, especially as all the details are missing. The vehicle is parked in Los Angeles, and you should also consider shipping costs, considering the overall condition of the car.
The listing expires in four weeks, and this is great news for every possible buyer, as this means they’re getting enough time to obtain all the information they need to make an informed decision.
